statement: How many different triangles have whole-number side lengths and a perimeter of 17? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count as the same.)

choices.misconception: I counted only triangles with three different side lengths and left out the isosceles ones.
I thought a side of length 1 could not belong to a triangle, so I left out the triangle with sides 1, 8 and 8.
I counted every way to split 17 into three whole-number lengths and never checked that they make a triangle.
I counted the same triangle again for every order of its side lengths.

hints: Organise by the length of the longest side.
Use the triangle inequality: the longest side must be less than the sum of the other two, so less than half the perimeter. Fix the longest side and list the other two in order.
The longest side c satisfies c < 17 - c, so c is at most 8, and it must be at least 6 since it is the largest of three numbers adding to 17.

solutions.reliable: Write the sides as a, b, c with a ≤ b ≤ c. The triangle inequality needs a + b > c, that is 17 - c > c, so c is at most 8; and c is at least 17 / 3, so c is 6, 7 or 8. For c = 8, a + b = 9 with b ≤ 8: 1, 8; 2, 7; 3, 6; 4, 5 (4 triangles). For c = 7, a + b = 10 with a ≤ b ≤ 7: 3, 7; 4, 6; 5, 5 (3 triangles). For c = 6, a + b = 11 with b ≤ 6: 5, 6 (1 triangle). Total 8. The transferable idea: fix the largest part first, because the triangle inequality only ever bites on the longest side.

whyOnTest: Triangle counts combine casework with the triangle inequality, and the choices catch every way of losing or doubling cases.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
